evidence.title: White House - Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: This week's Model Context Protocol security wave hardened a single conclusion: the layer that wires agents to tools is the AI stack's most exposed surface, and the fix is structural rather than per-server. Adversa's VIPER-MCP scanner swept roughly 40,000 MCP repositories into 106 zero-days and 67 CVEs - nine of them tracing to broken OAuth flows - while a Censys scan counted 12,520 internet-accessible MCP services that are mostly unauthenticated and a separate study found about 40% of remote MCP servers expose their tools with no authentication at all. The NSA's design-considerations document then supplied a government baseline naming the inverted client-server pattern, unverified task propagation, tool-poisoning, and arbitrary-code-execution as the protocol's core risks. The throughline is a zero-trust agenda: authenticate every remote MCP server, treat agent memory and MCP configuration as untrusted input, and inspect each agent-to-tool exchange. The durable way to enforce that is at the specification level, because optional, SHOULD-grade guidance is exactly what produced a population of unauthenticated public servers. The forward consequence is that the MCP specification itself stops leaving authentication and caller identity to the implementer and promotes them to a normative requirement for remote transports. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by H1 2027 a published revision of the official MCP specification makes authentication (or a verified identity/authorization handshake) a MUST-level requirement for remote/HTTP-transport servers - not merely an OPTIONAL or RECOMMENDED OAuth profile - so that a spec-compliant remote server can no longer expose tools with no authentication. Absent such a normative change in a dated, published spec revision by June 30, 2027, the prediction fails.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: MCP specification makes remote-server authentication mandatory by H1 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: CISA's June 9 addition of CVE-2026-42271 - the unauthenticated command-injection flaw in LiteLLM's MCP-server preview endpoints, chainable with a Starlette host-header bypass into CVSS 10.0 remote code execution - to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog is the moment the agent stack's tool-wiring layer crossed from security research into a confirmed, in-the-wild, federally-tracked exposure with a remediation deadline attached. LiteLLM is the open-source proxy that brokers calls across hundreds of model providers, so the host that gets compromised is precisely the one holding every connected service's provider credentials and API keys; this is the same exposed surface the week's broader MCP wave keeps naming - the 67-CVE VIPER-MCP sweep, the roughly 40% of remote MCP servers with no authentication, the NSA design-considerations baseline, and the Ollama memory-leak flaw. A single KEV entry patches one CVE; it does not yet establish that the AI agent-broker and MCP-configuration tier is a distinct, governed software class. The forward thesis is that the US federal cyber-governance machinery formalizes that class: CISA promotes its handling of LLM proxies and MCP-config servers from case-by-case KEV listings into standing, named guidance or a binding operational directive that treats internet-reachable AI inference proxies and agent-tool brokers as managed, high-value-credential software - patch on KEV timelines, keep off the public internet, authenticate every caller. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q2 2027 CISA (or a joint CISA-NSA publication) issues binding-directive-grade or formally published guidance that names AI inference proxies, LLM gateways, or MCP servers as an in-scope category subject to KEV-timeline remediation and internet-exposure restriction - not merely additional individual CVE listings. If by June 30, 2027 the only federal action is further per-CVE KEV entries with no category-level directive or named guidance for the agent-broker tier, the prediction fails. The counter-risk is that CISA keeps the layer inside generic web-application and KEV processes and never carves out a named AI-agent-infrastructure class.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: AI inference proxies gain named CISA KEV-timeline governance by Q2 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The Langflow case is not a one-off bug; it is a class signature. CVE-2026-55255 is a cross-tenant insecure-direct-object-reference (CWE-639, authorization bypass through a user-controlled key) on a flow-execution endpoint, rated CVSS 9.9 and now fired in the wild per Sysdig's June 25 report, chained with the already-KEV-listed RCE CVE-2026-33017. The structural read is that the soft underbelly of multi-tenant agent platforms is the orchestration and authorization plane: a visual builder that resolves another tenant's flow by an opaque, harvestable ID and never checks ownership turns the product into a cross-customer exfiltration primitive. The same architectural pattern — opaque flow/run/workspace IDs, a shared execution endpoint, owner checks deferred to UI rather than enforced server-side per object — recurs across the open-source and commercial peers in this category (the n8n / Flowise / Dify / LangGraph Platform / CrewAI class). The forward call: by Q1 2027 at least one OTHER named platform in this category (not Langflow) receives a CVSS >= 9.0 advisory whose root cause is cross-tenant authorization / broken-object-level access / IDOR, ideally with in-the-wild-exploitation or CISA-KEV evidence. The structural answer this pressures the category toward is zero-trust per-tenant gating: ownership enforced at the object boundary on every flow-resolution and run-execution path, not at the UI or the route prefix.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Multi-tenant agent builders draw a 9.0+ cross-tenant authz CVE by Q1 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: Anthropic published How we contain Claude across products on its engineering blog Saturday May 30, walking through the agent-isolation stack converged across all three product surfaces: gVisor containers with seccomp syscall filtering on isolated infrastructure for Claude.ai (ephemeral per-session filesystems), OS-native process sandboxes for Claude Code (Seatbelt on macOS and Bubblewrap on Linux, with an 84% reduction in permission prompts after delegating command approvals to a model-based classifier), and full guest VMs for Claude Cowork running on Apple Virtualization framework on macOS and Hyper-V HCS on Windows with host-held credentials and read-only / read-write / read-write-no-delete file-mount modes. The structural force is procurement-side. Once one frontier lab publicly commits to mature hypervisor + OS-sandbox + VM containment as the named posture and explicitly argues that the software you build yourself is often the weakest component, every peer agent-harness vendor faces a buyer-side question whose answer cannot stay opaque: does your harness ship equivalent containment, or do you document why not. The same convergence pressure that pulled SBOM formats and hyperscaler responsible-scaling templates into a small number of public shapes will act here, because enterprise security teams refuse to map N vendor-specific harness-isolation narratives into N risk-acceptance frameworks when the reference design is already public. By Q2 2027 we expect at least two of Cursor, Codex CLI, Cline, Windsurf, Devin, and Continue to publish named containment profiles matching the Anthropic posture (per-OS sandbox tier for the local CLI plus per-product VM tier for the autonomous-agent surface), and at least one standards body (OpenSSF, the CNCF agent SIG, or a Frontier Model Forum working group analog) to publish a draft agent-runtime-containment profile that names gVisor or equivalent at the cloud tier and named OS sandboxes at the laptop tier as the reference design. Bear case is a single peer vendor publishes a divergent containment spec (Wasm-only or eBPF-only) that fragments the convergence pressure before two named vendors align; absent that fragmentation, Q2 2027 lands the first peer-vendor containment specs and the first standards-body draft naming hypervisor + OS sandbox as the agent-runtime reference.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Agent-harness vendors ship gVisor+OS-sandbox+VM containment specs by Q2 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The agentic text-to-SQL execution layer will converge on a safe-by-default posture: by Q1 2027 at least three widely used LLM-agent frameworks beyond Langroid will ship their database-query tools defaulting to a parser-validated, SELECT-only allowlist with a dialect-aware dangerous-pattern blocklist, treating raw write/DDL/program-execution SQL as opt-in rather than the out-of-the-box behavior. The shift is driven by the realization that a model coerced via prompt injection can author arbitrary SQL, so the framework's own execution wrapper - not just the deployer's database role - must be the enforcement point. Expect this to show up concretely as a changed default in tools such as LangChain's SQL toolkit, LlamaIndex's text-to-SQL query engine, or comparable agent libraries, alongside documentation that elevates least-privilege, read-only database credentials from a footnote to a stated prerequisite. linked_predictions.prediction_summary: Simon Willison's datasette-agent 0.2a0, released June 10, adds a capability most autonomous-loop harnesses still lack: a tool that declares a context parameter receives a ToolContext object and can call await context.ask_user(...) to suspend the run and ask the operator a yes/no, multiple-choice, or free-text question instead of guessing, and the suspended conversation persists to the database and survives a server restart, so the half-finished run resumes once the human answers; a paired save_query tool writes agent-generated SQL as a stored query only after explicit human approval. This matters because it is not a UI confirmation popup but a durable, restart-surviving suspend/resume checkpoint implemented at the individual-tool level, which is exactly the human-in-the-loop primitive that durable-execution agent frameworks have been converging toward from the orchestration side. As agents move from chat into long-running unattended work, the failure mode shifts from a wrong answer to a wrong irreversible action taken with no chance to intervene, and the durable answer is to let any tool pause the loop, ask a question, and hold its state across process death until a person responds - a control surface that does not exist if the only checkpoints are ephemeral in-memory prompts that vanish on restart. The forward thesis is that this ask-user-and-survive-restart checkpoint hardens from a single open-source implementation into an expected, named feature of the major agent harnesses and coding-agent runtimes. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by H1 2027 at least two major agent harnesses or coding-agent frameworks (the strongest candidates being a Claude Code / Codex CLI / Cursor / Cline-class coding agent, an orchestration framework such as LangGraph or a durable-execution runtime like Temporal or Restate, or a managed agent platform like AWS Bedrock AgentCore or Microsoft Foundry) ship a documented mid-execution human-input primitive in which a running tool can suspend the agent, request a typed answer or approval from the operator, and resume the same run after a full process or server restart - state persisted, not re-prompted from scratch. A transient in-memory approval prompt, a pre-run permission allowlist, or an after-the-fact audit log does not count; the marker is a documented suspend-ask-resume checkpoint that durably survives restart, shipped by a non-Datasette stack.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: Unsloth's 2026.6.7 beta on June 12 did something the on-device fine-tuning stack had not done before: it made Google's text-diffusion language model DiffusionGemma directly runnable and trainable inside a downloadable local app, alongside Gemma 4 multi-token prediction, audio chat, and quantization-aware training that the team reports cuts memory roughly threefold. Text-diffusion language models - which denoise whole token blocks in parallel rather than generating left-to-right one token at a time - have until now lived almost entirely in research papers and hosted demos, with no first-class path to fine-tune them on consumer hardware. By absorbing DiffusionGemma into the same local toolchain that already handles autoregressive LoRA, speculative decoding, and post-training quantization, Unsloth turned the diffusion-LM from a paper curiosity into something a practitioner can actually post-train at home. The structural reason this is a seed rather than a one-off is that the rest of the local fine-tuning ecosystem - the runtimes (llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, MLX) and the other training libraries (Axolotl, TRL, torchtune) - currently has effectively no support for the diffusion-LM denoising graph, so the format ships against an ecosystem not yet built to run or train it, which is precisely the gap a category forms to fill. The forward thesis is that the open-weight, locally-trainable text-diffusion language model hardens into an established category rather than remaining a single DiffusionGemma-in-Unsloth checkpoint. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q2 2027 EITHER a second independent open-weight text-diffusion (discrete or continuous diffusion / masked-denoising) language-model family ships with its own model card and downloadable weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Google publisher whose generation is diffusion-based rather than autoregressive (candidates include Alibaba/Qwen, Mistral, Inception/Mercury-lineage groups, or an academic lab releasing open weights), OR a second mainstream local training or inference stack beyond Unsloth - llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, MLX, Axolotl, or TRL - ships first-class, documented support for fine-tuning or running a text-diffusion LM natively on consumer or edge hardware. A pure research paper with no released weights, a hosted-API-only diffusion model with no downloadable checkpoint, a further Google or Unsloth follow-up on DiffusionGemma itself, or a runtime that merely wraps Unsloth's existing path does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight diffusion-LM family or genuine second-stack local support for the diffusion-LM graph. If by June 30, 2027 DiffusionGemma-in-Unsloth remains the only locally-trainable open-weight text-diffusion LM and no second mainstream stack has shipped native support, the prediction fails.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: DiffusionGemma seeds an open-weight text-diffusion training category by Q2 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: Google's June 10 release of DiffusionGemma under Apache 2.0 is the moment open-weight text diffusion stopped being a research curiosity and shipped as a usable local model: a 26B Mixture-of-Experts (3.8B active) built on the Gemma 4 backbone with an added diffusion head, it abandons left-to-right autoregressive decoding to refine a 256-token block in parallel over multiple passes, locking in confident tokens as context for up to 4x faster generation, and it lands with native support across vLLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX, NVIDIA NeMo, and Unsloth, plus a shipped Unsloth Sudoku fine-tune that exploits its bidirectional attention. Two things make this a seed rather than a one-off. First, Google is explicit that output quality trails standard autoregressive Gemma 4 and steers production work back to the autoregressive model, positioning diffusion squarely for speed-critical, low-concurrency local inference - the exact envelope an edge runtime is built to fill. Second, the on-device stack is not yet ready for it: llama.cpp support is listed only as coming, so the GGUF/CPU path where Gemma-class weights are actually deployed locally cannot run block-parallel diffusion decoding on launch day, and the open-weight text-diffusion field has exactly one member. The forward thesis is that text diffusion hardens into an established open-weight model category rather than remaining a single Google checkpoint. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q1 2027 EITHER a second independent major open-weight text-diffusion language model ships with its own model card and weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Google publisher (the strongest candidates being Alibaba/Qwen, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral, or NVIDIA), OR a mainstream on-device inference runtime that did not support it at DiffusionGemma's launch - llama.cpp foremost, or LM Studio, Ollama, or MLX as a packaged GGUF/edge path - ships first-class block-parallel text-diffusion decoding so the format runs on the consumer CPU/edge stack. A research-only paper with no released weights, a one-off Google follow-up checkpoint, or a runtime that merely wraps the existing PyTorch path without native diffusion-decoding support does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight diffusion-LLM release or genuine edge-runtime support for the decoding scheme. If by March 31, 2027 DiffusionGemma is still the only open-weight text-diffusion model and no mainstream on-device runtime has added native diffusion decoding, the prediction fails.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The Great American AI Act discussion draft conditions its three-year preemption of state development laws on a new federal disclosure: any frontier developer above roughly $500M in prior-year gross revenue must publish a public framework describing how it evaluates and manages a model's catastrophic risks. Several of the labs that clear that threshold already maintain their own catastrophic-risk safety frameworks under different names and structures, so the draft's mandatory-disclosure shape gives them a strong incentive to act before a bill is ever voted on. The prediction is that the largest frontier developers will voluntarily revise and re-publish their existing safety frameworks to converge on a common disclosure structure that mirrors the draft's framework requirement, treating the bill text as the template the industry standardizes around. Moving first lets the labs define what a compliant catastrophic-risk disclosure looks like, blunt the safety-advocate argument that a federal ceiling weakens the state-law floor, and lock in a uniform regime they can defend in lobbying as the draft moves toward formal introduction. Concretely, by the second quarter of 2027 at least three over-threshold developers will publish framework updates that explicitly track the federal disclosure shape, well ahead of any enacted statutory deadline.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Frontier-lab safety frameworks align on catastrophic-risk disclosure by Q2 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: A new arxiv benchmark, DeployBench, reframes where autonomous coding agents are actually breaking: not on writing code, but on getting an existing research artifact to run on a fresh machine. Across 51 environment-setup tasks spanning multi-language toolchains, GPU/CUDA, kernel configuration, and legacy compatibility, four state-of-the-art models inside the OpenHands harness scored only 7.8% to 51.0%, and the dominant failure was not missing capability but a "completion-judgment problem" - agent-terminated self-stops where the agent's own pre-finish checks declared success against a weaker or different target than the task required. Because that failure mode is a property of the harness, not the underlying model, it is fixable at the framework layer, and it maps to a feature competitors can ship and market. The prediction: by H1 2027 at least two major coding-agent frameworks will make goal-grounded completion verification a default - the agent must execute the task's real target (run the artifact, pass the specified check) before it is permitted to report done, rather than trusting a self-authored proxy check - and research-artifact / environment-setup deployment will appear as a standard axis in agent evaluation suites, not just functional code generation.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Coding-agent frameworks ship goal-grounded completion verification by H1 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: OpenAI's Frontier Governance Framework is the first public lab document to anchor systemic risk to specific quantitative thresholds — greater than 50 fatalities or $1 billion in property damages from a single incident — and to bind those numbers to SB 53's annual-update cycle and the EU AI Act Code of Practice's reporting obligations. Once one frontier lab publishes a numeric harm floor inside a regulator-facing document, the other Tier-1 labs (Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI, Mistral) lose the option of vague qualitative language: their existing responsible-scaling and preparedness policies will be benchmarked against OpenAI's numbers by California AG staff drafting SB 53 implementation guidance, by EU AI Office reviewers scoring CoP signatories, and by enterprise procurement teams writing model-risk clauses. The forcing function is mechanical — SB 53 requires annual updates, the EU CoP requires alignment statements, and enterprise contracts are now citing specific lab frameworks by name. By Q2 2027 we expect at least three of the Tier-1 labs to have published Frontier-Governance-Framework-equivalents that either adopt OpenAI's 50-fatalities / $1B-damages threshold pair verbatim, propose a competing pair with explicit justification for the delta, or jointly publish a reconciled threshold standard under an industry body (likely the Frontier Model Forum given its existing OpenAI-Anthropic-Google-Microsoft membership). The reconciled-standard branch becomes increasingly likely as enterprise customers refuse to maintain N different risk-acceptance frameworks across N model vendors.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Frontier-lab governance frameworks converge on shared quantitative-harm thresholds by Q2 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The AI-accelerator and custom-ASIC equity complex now reacts to in-line guidance the way it once reacted to a miss, and that asymmetry is the prediction's engine. Broadcom's fiscal-Q2 report beat on revenue and EPS but guided Q3 AI-semiconductor revenue to roughly $16 billion against a roughly $17.2 billion consensus and pointedly declined to raise its full-year 2026 AI forecast; the stock fell about 15% and pulled the rest of the group down for two straight sessions (Micron, Intel, AMD, and Nvidia all lower), with a deepening memory-pricing crisis compounding the move. The structural read is that these names are priced for continuous beat-and-raise, so a merely-solid quarter is repriced as a disappointment and the correlation drags peers with it. The forecast: the next major custom-ASIC or merchant-accelerator print that meets-not-raises - the subsequent Broadcom, Marvell, AMD, or Nvidia data-center update - triggers a repeat of this pattern by Q4 2026, namely a double-digit single-session drop in the reporting name accompanied by a correlated sell-off across the accelerator and high-bandwidth-memory peers, alongside visible sell-side estimate cuts or a coverage re-rating that trims AI-chip revenue and target assumptions for the group. What breaks the thesis is a clean beat-and-raise from the next reporter that re-anchors expectations upward, or a print that misses outright (which would make any drawdown a fundamentals story rather than the expectations-asymmetry story this prediction is about); what confirms it is an in-line guide that still clears the prior quarter yet sells off on the gap to a raised bar.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: AI-accelerator equities re-rate lower on the next in-line ASIC print by Q4 2026

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The largest demands on US public-market capital are converging on a single thesis at once: that owning compute — rockets, frontier models, and the data centers behind them — is the trade of the cycle. SpaceX has fixed its IPO at $135 a share before the roadshow even begins, an unusual pre-commitment that points to roughly $75 billion raised on about 555.5 million shares at a ~$1.77 trillion valuation, slated to price around June 11 and debut around June 12 on Nasdaq as SPCX — the largest IPO in US history. It does not land alone. Anthropic has already confidentially filed a draft S-1 after a May round valued it at $965 billion (up from $380 billion in February), and OpenAI is reported to be preparing its own confidential filing within weeks. When this much primary issuance, all underwritten by the same handful of syndicate banks and all sold on a correlated compute narrative, queues into a few months, the supply has to be absorbed by a buyer base whose AI exposure is already concentrated. The mechanical consequence is crowding: to fund tens of billions in new SPCX stock plus whatever frontier-lab paper follows, allocators rotate out of existing AI-correlated holdings, and the marginal price of the thesis gets tested rather than assumed. The prediction is that this concentration produces a measurable crowding signal in the SpaceX pricing-and-debut window and the weeks after — a compute-correlated issuer that prices below its marketed range, trims its raise, or slips its timetable, or an observable drawdown in a basket of already-public AI-infrastructure names as the SPCX print clears. The forward state to watch is not whether these companies eventually list — the filings make that near-certain — but whether the market can take down this much same-thesis supply without repricing it, and the first dislocation is the tell.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Compute-thesis IPO supply triggers measurable AI-equity crowding by Q4 2026

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: When AMD takes the stage at Advancing AI 2026 on July 22-23 at Moscone Center, expect the MI400 pitch to lead with memory rather than raw compute. The generational story reporting points to is a bandwidth jump of more than 2x over MI350, built on CDNA 5 and TSMC's 2nm node, with the rack-scale 'Helios' system and the availability timelines held back at the 2025 preview finally detailed. The framing matters because the binding constraint in inference has shifted: long-context workloads inflate KV-cache footprints, so buyers increasingly value larger HBM pools and smarter parallelism over headline FLOPS. That same logic explains NVIDIA's counter-positioning, with Blackwell Ultra GB300 reaching 288GB of HBM3e and Rubin Ultra variants targeting 512GB. With HBM capacity reportedly sold out through calendar 2026 and TAM projected near $100B by 2028, the top of the accelerator market is settling into a memory-capacity and bandwidth contest, and AMD's July reveal is the near-term catalyst that makes that reframing explicit.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The Model Context Protocol's stdio transport will lose its status as an unguarded shell into the host process. By Q2 2027 at least three widely used MCP hosts or agent frameworks will ship their stdio tool-server path defaulting to an isolated execution boundary - a separate process or container with a constrained environment, an explicit per-server command allowlist, and dropped privileges - rather than spawning an attacker-configurable command in the host's own context. The change is forced by the recognition that the stdio adapter exists precisely to run code, so an allowlist-and-flag-validation patch over a single field cannot be the whole defense; the enforcement point has to be the runtime that launches and confines the tool, not the string it was handed. Concretely, expect this to surface as a changed default in the reference servers and SDKs and in popular flow builders, with documentation that reframes remote transports and process isolation as the recommended posture and treats raw in-host stdio exec as an opt-in for trusted local setups only. Frameworks that keep launching tool commands directly inside the agent process will keep drawing their own critical advisories as researchers replay the one-click configuration-to-execution pattern across the ecosystem.

Microsoft did not fork OpenClaw into a hidden internal stack; it shipped the open harness as the runtime and layered enterprise controls on top, so each Scout agent runs under a governed Entra identity with scoped credentials and audit trails, a continuous policy-conformance check, Purview data-protection enforcement before data leaves, and a Work IQ context layer. The reason this generalizes is that the hard, differentiated work for an enterprise vendor is now the governance wrapper, identity, and product surface, while the agent loop itself is a solved, battle-tested open component a vendor can adopt rather than rebuild. That inverts the old build-versus-buy calculus for the engine: reimplementing a proprietary agent runtime offers little advantage over embedding a maintained open harness and competing on controls and distribution. The forward state to watch is therefore a second first-party branded agent from a major platform or productivity vendor that discloses one of the tracked open harnesses (OpenClaw or a peer) as its underlying runtime, wrapped in that vendor's own identity, policy, and data-governance controls. The confirming signal is a launch, preview, or technical disclosure naming a specific open harness as the engine inside a branded enterprise agent; the pattern fails to confirm if rival vendors instead ship agents on closed in-house runtimes through year end.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: Zyphra's June 12 release of Zamba2-VL under Apache 2.0 is the moment the state-space-hybrid backbone crossed from text into open-weight multimodal at sizes that actually fit local hardware. The family ships at 1.2B, 2.7B, and 7B with checkpoints on Hugging Face: the language backbone interleaves Mamba2 state-space layers with a small number of shared transformer blocks, and the vision side reuses the Vision Transformer from Qwen2.5-VL through a two-layer MLP adapter. The payoff is latency - on a 32K-token prefill Zyphra measures roughly an order-of-magnitude lower time-to-first-token than comparable transformer VLMs, the regime that decides whether on-device document and screen understanding feels instant - and the small models are not merely competitive but strong on perception, with the 1.2B variant reaching PixMoCount 62.5, nearly double the transformer-based InternVL3.5-1B at 32.8, and the 2.7B/7B variants posting CountBenchQA 87.5 and 90.6. Two things make this a seed rather than a one-off. First, the value proposition is structural, not incidental: linear-time state-space attention is exactly what removes the quadratic prefill cost that makes long-context, image-heavy VLMs slow on edge silicon, so the architecture's advantage compounds precisely where local multimodal inference is headed. Second, the field has exactly one open-weight SSM-hybrid VLM family today, and the on-device runtime stack that actually deploys 1-7B weights locally - llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio - has no first-class path for the Mamba2-hybrid VLM graph, so the format ships against an ecosystem not yet built to run it. The forward thesis is that the SSM-hybrid multimodal backbone hardens into an established open-weight edge category rather than remaining a single Zyphra checkpoint. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q2 2027 EITHER a second independent open-weight SSM-hybrid (Mamba/state-space) vision-language model family ships with its own model card and downloadable weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Zyphra publisher (the strongest candidates being Alibaba/Qwen, Mistral, NVIDIA, AI21, or a Mamba-lineage group), OR a mainstream on-device/edge inference runtime that did not support it at Zamba2-VL's launch - llama.cpp foremost, or Ollama, LM Studio, or MLX as a packaged GGUF/edge path - ships first-class support for the Mamba2-hybrid VLM path so the model runs natively on the consumer/edge stack. A pure-text SSM model with no vision tower, a research-only paper with no released weights, a further Zyphra follow-up checkpoint, or a runtime that merely wraps the existing custom transformers fork without native Mamba2-hybrid VLM support does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight SSM-hybrid VLM family or genuine edge-runtime support for the hybrid multimodal graph. If by June 30, 2027 Zamba2-VL is still the only open-weight SSM-hybrid VLM family and no mainstream on-device runtime has shipped first-class support for the Mamba2-hybrid VLM path, the prediction fails.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: SSM-hybrid open-weight VLMs harden into an established edge category by Q2 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: Google's June 10 release of DiffusionGemma under Apache 2.0 is the moment open-weight text diffusion stopped being a research curiosity and shipped as a usable local model: a 26B Mixture-of-Experts (3.8B active) built on the Gemma 4 backbone with an added diffusion head, it abandons left-to-right autoregressive decoding to refine a 256-token block in parallel over multiple passes, locking in confident tokens as context for up to 4x faster generation, and it lands with native support across vLLM, Hugging Face Transformers, MLX, NVIDIA NeMo, and Unsloth, plus a shipped Unsloth Sudoku fine-tune that exploits its bidirectional attention. Two things make this a seed rather than a one-off. First, Google is explicit that output quality trails standard autoregressive Gemma 4 and steers production work back to the autoregressive model, positioning diffusion squarely for speed-critical, low-concurrency local inference - the exact envelope an edge runtime is built to fill. Second, the on-device stack is not yet ready for it: llama.cpp support is listed only as coming, so the GGUF/CPU path where Gemma-class weights are actually deployed locally cannot run block-parallel diffusion decoding on launch day, and the open-weight text-diffusion field has exactly one member. The forward thesis is that text diffusion hardens into an established open-weight model category rather than remaining a single Google checkpoint. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q1 2027 EITHER a second independent major open-weight text-diffusion language model ships with its own model card and weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Google publisher (the strongest candidates being Alibaba/Qwen, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral, or NVIDIA), OR a mainstream on-device inference runtime that did not support it at DiffusionGemma's launch - llama.cpp foremost, or LM Studio, Ollama, or MLX as a packaged GGUF/edge path - ships first-class block-parallel text-diffusion decoding so the format runs on the consumer CPU/edge stack. A research-only paper with no released weights, a one-off Google follow-up checkpoint, or a runtime that merely wraps the existing PyTorch path without native diffusion-decoding support does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight diffusion-LLM release or genuine edge-runtime support for the decoding scheme. If by March 31, 2027 DiffusionGemma is still the only open-weight text-diffusion model and no mainstream on-device runtime has added native diffusion decoding, the prediction fails.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Open-weight text-diffusion LLMs add a second family or edge runtime by Q1 2027

The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q1 2027 EITHER a second independent major open-weight text-diffusion language model ships with its own model card and weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Google publisher (the strongest candidates being Alibaba/Qwen, Meta, DeepSeek, Mistral, or NVIDIA), OR a mainstream on-device inference runtime that did not support it at DiffusionGemma's launch - llama.cpp foremost, or LM Studio, Ollama, or MLX as a packaged GGUF/edge path - ships first-class block-parallel text-diffusion decoding so the format runs on the consumer CPU/edge stack. A research-only paper with no released weights, a one-off Google follow-up checkpoint, or a runtime that merely wraps the existing PyTorch path without native diffusion-decoding support does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight diffusion-LLM release or genuine edge-runtime support for the decoding scheme. If by March 31, 2027 DiffusionGemma is still the only open-weight text-diffusion model and no mainstream on-device runtime has added native diffusion decoding, the prediction fails.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Open-weight text-diffusion LLMs add a second family or edge runtime by Q1 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: Unsloth's 2026.6.7 beta on June 12 did something the on-device fine-tuning stack had not done before: it made Google's text-diffusion language model DiffusionGemma directly runnable and trainable inside a downloadable local app, alongside Gemma 4 multi-token prediction, audio chat, and quantization-aware training that the team reports cuts memory roughly threefold. Text-diffusion language models - which denoise whole token blocks in parallel rather than generating left-to-right one token at a time - have until now lived almost entirely in research papers and hosted demos, with no first-class path to fine-tune them on consumer hardware. By absorbing DiffusionGemma into the same local toolchain that already handles autoregressive LoRA, speculative decoding, and post-training quantization, Unsloth turned the diffusion-LM from a paper curiosity into something a practitioner can actually post-train at home. The structural reason this is a seed rather than a one-off is that the rest of the local fine-tuning ecosystem - the runtimes (llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, MLX) and the other training libraries (Axolotl, TRL, torchtune) - currently has effectively no support for the diffusion-LM denoising graph, so the format ships against an ecosystem not yet built to run or train it, which is precisely the gap a category forms to fill. The forward thesis is that the open-weight, locally-trainable text-diffusion language model hardens into an established category rather than remaining a single DiffusionGemma-in-Unsloth checkpoint. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by Q2 2027 EITHER a second independent open-weight text-diffusion (discrete or continuous diffusion / masked-denoising) language-model family ships with its own model card and downloadable weights under a permissive or open license from a non-Google publisher whose generation is diffusion-based rather than autoregressive (candidates include Alibaba/Qwen, Mistral, Inception/Mercury-lineage groups, or an academic lab releasing open weights), OR a second mainstream local training or inference stack beyond Unsloth - llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, MLX, Axolotl, or TRL - ships first-class, documented support for fine-tuning or running a text-diffusion LM natively on consumer or edge hardware. A pure research paper with no released weights, a hosted-API-only diffusion model with no downloadable checkpoint, a further Google or Unsloth follow-up on DiffusionGemma itself, or a runtime that merely wraps Unsloth's existing path does not count; the marker is a second independent open-weight diffusion-LM family or genuine second-stack local support for the diffusion-LM graph. If by June 30, 2027 DiffusionGemma-in-Unsloth remains the only locally-trainable open-weight text-diffusion LM and no second mainstream stack has shipped native support, the prediction fails.

Broadcom's fiscal-Q2 report beat on revenue and EPS but guided Q3 AI-semiconductor revenue to roughly $16 billion against a roughly $17.2 billion consensus and pointedly declined to raise its full-year 2026 AI forecast; the stock fell about 15% and pulled the rest of the group down for two straight sessions (Micron, Intel, AMD, and Nvidia all lower), with a deepening memory-pricing crisis compounding the move. The forecast: the next major custom-ASIC or merchant-accelerator print that meets-not-raises - the subsequent Broadcom, Marvell, AMD, or Nvidia data-center update - triggers a repeat of this pattern by Q4 2026, namely a double-digit single-session drop in the reporting name accompanied by a correlated sell-off across the accelerator and high-bandwidth-memory peers, alongside visible sell-side estimate cuts or a coverage re-rating that trims AI-chip revenue and target assumptions for the group. linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The largest demands on US public-market capital are converging on a single thesis at once: that owning compute — rockets, frontier models, and the data centers behind them — is the trade of the cycle. SpaceX has fixed its IPO at $135 a share before the roadshow even begins, an unusual pre-commitment that points to roughly $75 billion raised on about 555.5 million shares at a ~$1.77 trillion valuation, slated to price around June 11 and debut around June 12 on Nasdaq as SPCX — the largest IPO in US history. It does not land alone. Anthropic has already confidentially filed a draft S-1 after a May round valued it at $965 billion (up from $380 billion in February), and OpenAI is reported to be preparing its own confidential filing within weeks. When this much primary issuance, all underwritten by the same handful of syndicate banks and all sold on a correlated compute narrative, queues into a few months, the supply has to be absorbed by a buyer base whose AI exposure is already concentrated. The mechanical consequence is crowding: to fund tens of billions in new SPCX stock plus whatever frontier-lab paper follows, allocators rotate out of existing AI-correlated holdings, and the marginal price of the thesis gets tested rather than assumed. The prediction is that this concentration produces a measurable crowding signal in the SpaceX pricing-and-debut window and the weeks after — a compute-correlated issuer that prices below its marketed range, trims its raise, or slips its timetable, or an observable drawdown in a basket of already-public AI-infrastructure names as the SPCX print clears. The forward state to watch is not whether these companies eventually list — the filings make that near-certain — but whether the market can take down this much same-thesis supply without repricing it, and the first dislocation is the tell.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Compute-thesis IPO supply triggers measurable AI-equity crowding by Q4 2026

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The Model Context Protocol's stdio transport will lose its status as an unguarded shell into the host process. By Q2 2027 at least three widely used MCP hosts or agent frameworks will ship their stdio tool-server path defaulting to an isolated execution boundary - a separate process or container with a constrained environment, an explicit per-server command allowlist, and dropped privileges - rather than spawning an attacker-configurable command in the host's own context. The change is forced by the recognition that the stdio adapter exists precisely to run code, so an allowlist-and-flag-validation patch over a single field cannot be the whole defense; the enforcement point has to be the runtime that launches and confines the tool, not the string it was handed. Concretely, expect this to surface as a changed default in the reference servers and SDKs and in popular flow builders, with documentation that reframes remote transports and process isolation as the recommended posture and treats raw in-host stdio exec as an opt-in for trusted local setups only. Frameworks that keep launching tool commands directly inside the agent process will keep drawing their own critical advisories as researchers replay the one-click configuration-to-execution pattern across the ecosystem.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The June 12 arXiv paper CacheRL (arXiv:2606.14179) attacks the most expensive part of teaching a small model to use tools well: reinforcement learning over multi-turn tool use normally has to run the real tools live thousands of times per training batch, which dominates cost and makes the loop slow and brittle. CacheRL removes the live tool calls by replaying a three-tier fuzzy cache of past trajectories with token-level masking, and pairs that with a cache-tier-aware hybrid reward that reweights answer quality so the model is not punished for gaps the cache itself introduced. The reported numbers are the kind that get a method copied rather than admired: 92% process accuracy on multi-step tool-calling, within striking distance of GPT-5's reported 94%, while using roughly 100x less compute, and lifting validation reward on Qwen3-4B-Thinking from 0.43 to 0.78, with ablations crediting a 17% gain to the cache-aware reward. The structural reason this spreads is that the bottleneck it removes is universal: every team doing agent RL on open models — and the major open post-training libraries (TRL, verl, OpenRLHF, SkyRL, ART, NeMo-RL) plus inference-coupled rollout stacks — pays the same live-tool-execution tax, and a cached-replay rollout with a tier-aware reward is a drop-in substitution for the rollout phase rather than a new model architecture, which is exactly the shape of technique that diffuses fast. The forward thesis is that cached-rollout (replay-instead-of-live-execution) RL for tool-calling agents hardens from a single paper into a supported training mode that practitioners can pick up off the shelf. The concrete, falsifiable landing: by H1 2027 (on or before 2027-06-30) EITHER a mainstream open agent-RL or post-training framework other than the CacheRL authors' own code — TRL, verl, OpenRLHF, SkyRL, ART, NeMo-RL, or a comparably adopted open library — ships documented, first-class support for a cached or replayed rollout mode (offline trajectory replay with masking in place of live tool execution) for multi-turn tool-calling RL, OR at least one independent group publishes a reproduction that releases open weights or training code applying cached-rollout RL to a different base model family and reports tool-calling accuracy within ten points of a frontier model at an order-of-magnitude-lower rollout cost. What does NOT count: a closed or hosted-only service that merely offers 'cheaper agent RL' without a documented cached-replay rollout path; a generic prompt or trajectory cache used only for inference rather than for the RL rollout loop; a citation, benchmark mention, or blog reference to CacheRL with no shipped feature or released artifact; or a follow-up from the original authors on the same codebase. If by June 30, 2027 cached-rollout RL remains confined to the original CacheRL paper and its own repository, with no second framework feature and no independent open reproduction on a different model, the prediction fails.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: A purpose-built AI inference accelerator will ship or be unveiled with confidential computing as a named, load-bearing feature of the part itself — on-die root-of-trust, TEE-I/O so the model weights and activations stay encrypted in use across the CPU-accelerator boundary, and signed-model attestation that lets a tenant cryptographically verify which weights are running before sending data — marketed as a named confidential-inference SKU or managed tier by H1 2027. The June 24 OpenAI-Broadcom Jalapeno unveiling proved that buyer-designed rack-scale inference silicon is now real, but it disclosed no security-silicon angle, leaving an explicit gap: the inference accelerator wave so far competes on performance-per-watt and fabric bandwidth, not on confidentiality of the model and the prompt. Two structural forces close that gap. First, the same regulated and sovereign buyers driving custom-silicon economics also carry the heaviest data-residency and IP-protection requirements, and merchant accelerators already carry the primitives (NVIDIA Confidential Computing on Hopper/Blackwell, AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX with TEE-I/O) waiting to be productized into a named inference tier rather than a developer-preview flag. Second, the agentic-AI security cycle keeps tying risk to model-supply-chain integrity (poisoned checkpoints, unauthenticated registries), and signed-model attestation is the hardware-rooted answer to 'prove the weights I am querying are the weights I approved.' The falsifiable core is a NAMED part or managed tier where confidential inference — encrypted-in-use weights plus tenant-verifiable attestation — is the marketed feature, disclosed at a venue such as AMD Advancing AI (July 22-23), Hot Chips (August 23-25), Black Hat (August), or a hyperscaler launch. What does NOT count: a generic 'we support confidential computing' line on a GPU spec sheet with no inference-specific tier; a research paper or preprint with no shipping part; a confidential-VM offering that merely runs an unmodified accelerator without TEE-I/O or model attestation; or a restatement of an existing developer-preview that was already announced before today.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: AI accelerator ships confidential-inference tier with attestation by H1 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security executive order is written to be light-touch on its face: it explicitly bars any reading that authorizes mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting, and the frontier-model early-access track is framed as strictly voluntary. The teeth arrive through a different channel. The order directs Treasury, NSA, and CISA to build a benchmarking process, designate covered frontier models by reference to their offensive and defensive cyber capability, and stand up an AI Cybersecurity Clearinghouse that coordinates vulnerability scanning and patch distribution across federal and critical-infrastructure systems the government itself buys. That combination - a government-run designation list plus federal buying power flowing through the clearinghouse - is the classic path by which a nominally voluntary framework becomes a de facto seller requirement. The prediction is that by Q2 2027 the executive branch converts the framework into a procurement condition: a Federal Acquisition Regulation amendment, an agency acquisition rule, or standardized solicitation clause will require vendors of covered frontier models selling into federal use to attest that they participate in the cyber-capability benchmarking and the early-access disclosure process, with at least three covered-frontier vendors publishing such attestations or winning awards bound to the clause. This mirrors how prior cyber executive orders (secure-software self-attestation under the CISA repository) turned guidance into a contracting gate without new statute, and it is the executive-branch counterpart to the separate congressional catastrophic-risk disclosure debate rather than a restatement of it.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The largest demands on US public-market capital are converging on a single thesis at once: that owning compute — rockets, frontier models, and the data centers behind them — is the trade of the cycle. SpaceX has fixed its IPO at $135 a share before the roadshow even begins, an unusual pre-commitment that points to roughly $75 billion raised on about 555.5 million shares at a ~$1.77 trillion valuation, slated to price around June 11 and debut around June 12 on Nasdaq as SPCX — the largest IPO in US history. It does not land alone. Anthropic has already confidentially filed a draft S-1 after a May round valued it at $965 billion (up from $380 billion in February), and OpenAI is reported to be preparing its own confidential filing within weeks. When this much primary issuance, all underwritten by the same handful of syndicate banks and all sold on a correlated compute narrative, queues into a few months, the supply has to be absorbed by a buyer base whose AI exposure is already concentrated. The mechanical consequence is crowding: to fund tens of billions in new SPCX stock plus whatever frontier-lab paper follows, allocators rotate out of existing AI-correlated holdings, and the marginal price of the thesis gets tested rather than assumed. The prediction is that this concentration produces a measurable crowding signal in the SpaceX pricing-and-debut window and the weeks after — a compute-correlated issuer that prices below its marketed range, trims its raise, or slips its timetable, or an observable drawdown in a basket of already-public AI-infrastructure names as the SPCX print clears. The forward state to watch is not whether these companies eventually list — the filings make that near-certain — but whether the market can take down this much same-thesis supply without repricing it, and the first dislocation is the tell.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Compute-thesis IPO supply triggers measurable AI-equity crowding by Q4 2026

The release lands as a concept release rather than a proposed rule because the disclosure question crosses Reg S-K Item 101 / Item 303 / Item 11(h) and the staff needs comment-period input before drafting. linked_predictions.prediction_summary: A new arxiv benchmark, DeployBench, reframes where autonomous coding agents are actually breaking: not on writing code, but on getting an existing research artifact to run on a fresh machine. Across 51 environment-setup tasks spanning multi-language toolchains, GPU/CUDA, kernel configuration, and legacy compatibility, four state-of-the-art models inside the OpenHands harness scored only 7.8% to 51.0%, and the dominant failure was not missing capability but a "completion-judgment problem" - agent-terminated self-stops where the agent's own pre-finish checks declared success against a weaker or different target than the task required. Because that failure mode is a property of the harness, not the underlying model, it is fixable at the framework layer, and it maps to a feature competitors can ship and market. The prediction: by H1 2027 at least two major coding-agent frameworks will make goal-grounded completion verification a default - the agent must execute the task's real target (run the artifact, pass the specified check) before it is permitted to report done, rather than trusting a self-authored proxy check - and research-artifact / environment-setup deployment will appear as a standard axis in agent evaluation suites, not just functional code generation.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: Coding-agent frameworks ship goal-grounded completion verification by H1 2027

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: The Commerce OIG report published today June 1 names four NIST failures driving the National Vulnerability Database backlog past 27,000 unprocessed vulnerabilities — no formal NVD strategy, duplicate severity scoring on 80% of submissions already carrying scores, redundant CISA / NIST enrichment without coordination, and stakeholder updates lagging operational reality — with projected 2026 CVE volume above 60,000 and NIST under a July 25 2026 deadline to submit a formal action plan. On the same day Microsoft moved Defender Vulnerability Management's exposure score off raw CVSS dependence, blending EPSS exploit-likelihood signals, internet-facing posture, and asset-criticality weights into a single representative score that answers where to remediate first rather than how severe a CVE is in the abstract. By H1 2027 we expect three first-of-kind anchors to land in one window: (1) the first FFIEC Cyber Resilience handbook update naming AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and triage — Project Glasswing's 10,000+ findings cohort, the OpenSSF agent-runtime template, or an equivalent named program — as a defensible mitigating control inside an examination handbook section; (2) the first SEC Division of Corporation Finance Compliance and Disclosure Interpretation naming the operational status of an issuer's CVE-prioritization stack, not raw NVD enrichment volume, as the relevant baseline for Item 1.05 cyber-materiality and Item 106 risk-management disclosures under Reg S-K; (3) the first cyber-insurance carrier endorsement filing at a state department of insurance citing AI-assisted vuln discovery plus EPSS-weighted prioritization as a rated mitigating control inside the policy form. The structural force is non-transferability. A NIST contract cleanup that hits the July 25 action plan does not unlock financial-regulator examination relief, a FFIEC handbook update does not preempt SEC disclosure obligations, and a cyber-insurance endorsement does not retire CISA / NIST enrichment redundancy — the four problems the OIG named are jurisdictional, not technical, so each regulator has to write its own baseline against the same broken pipeline. The forcing function is mechanical: the NVD backlog is now larger than any single contractor cohort can re-enrich on the current FY27 budget envelope, FFIEC's Cyber Resilience Section refresh cycle has a 2027 update slot already open, and SEC Item 1.05 enforcement has been live since December 2023 with no Commission-staff guidance on what an issuer's vuln-prioritization stack must look like. The bear case is a triple slip — FFIEC sequences into 2028 behind the CSF 2.0 cross-walk refresh, the SEC C&DI gets bundled into a broader cyber-materiality concept release past Q3 2027, and the first carrier endorsement filing draws a state-DOI comment letter that delays the form; absent that triple slip, H1 2027 lands the first FFIEC reference, first SEC C&DI, and first carrier endorsement together as the federal-financial-insurer compliance baseline every CISO and audit committee has to plan against.

linked_predictions.prediction_summary: AWS unveiled Continuum at its New York Summit as an AI-native, model-agnostic vulnerability-management service whose defining move is validation by construction: rather than ranking findings by a static CVSS score, it builds a working exploit in a sandbox to prove a finding is genuinely reachable and exploitable before it ever reaches a human, filtering false positives and prioritizing by real production and business impact. This prediction holds that exploit-validation-as-a-stage stops being one hyperscaler's differentiator and becomes the expected baseline for AI-driven application-security tooling: by the first half of 2027 at least three additional named vendors or platforms in the AI code-security and ASPM space (for example incumbent SAST/ASPM vendors, an autonomous-pentest startup, or a rival cloud) will ship or document a feature that automatically constructs and runs a sandboxed proof-of-exploit to confirm a finding before surfacing it, rather than only scoring or de-duplicating alerts. The driver is the alert-fatigue economics that Continuum is explicitly built to attack: security teams drowning in unreachable, unexploitable findings will not pay for yet another scanner that adds noise, so the competitive frontier shifts from how many issues a tool finds to how few false alarms it forwards, and machine-built proof-of-exploit is the cheapest credible way to make that guarantee. The autonomous-pentesting tooling already visible at adjacent venues, such as the live offensive-security agent demos on this week's calendar, supplies the technical substrate that makes broad adoption plausible within the window.
linked_predictions.prediction_short_label: AWS Continuum's sandbox exploit-validation goes industry baseline by H1 2027
